January 2
Christmas 2C — The Second Sunday of Christmas
Colors: white, gold
Jer 31:7-14
Psalm 84
Eph 1:3-14
Lk 2:22-40, alt: Mt 2:1-12
Grace and peace from God Our Father and Our Lord, Jesus Christ in whom our trust never fails us.

There is nothing more fun than preparing a homily. Actually, now that I think about it, there are several things more fun than preparing a homily, and I suppose that may be the reason many of us put it off as long as we can. But, but, but... when I stumble across something completely new to me, it is quite exciting. I came across something completely new to me while I was working on why we celebrate the Feast of the Holy Name of Jesus. The best short answer to why we celebrate the circumcision of Jesus was best explained by Fr. Edward Looney [[https://soundcloud.com/fr-edward-looney/power-in-holy-name-of-jesus]]. In the culture we live in, the word "God" and the name "Jesus Christ" is held in low esteem. They are more likely to be found in cussing than in praise. Christians should find this very sad. St. Paul, in his letter to the Philippians, writes...

    Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. (Philippians 2:9-12).

Using Jesus' name in cussing is such common practice, I do not think quoting the above verse will make much of an impact on the secular world. Even so, I am determined to bow my head in reverence at the mention of Jesus' name, regardless of the context. The Feast of the Holy Name of Jesus reminds us his name is holy and should be respected, at least by those who follow him.

I was still left wondering why St. Luke thought this episode in Jesus' life was so important when the other Gospel writers didn't bother to mention it. There is the dedication to Theophilus in the first chapter wherein St. Luke proposes to write an orderly account. Speculations as to who Theophilus is are rampant, ranging from a specific person all the way to St. Luke's version of saying, "you, dear reader." For the record, I lean towards the you-dear-reader camp without being particularly convinced one way or the other.

Whoever St. Luke is addressing, he sounds as if he is addressing someone who is vaguely familiar with Christianity but lacks details. If that is the case, it seems reasonable on his part to include extra details about where Jesus came from, and thus, we get more specifics about Jesus' origins.

One of the things I noticed was how important a role *the elderly* played in these first few chapters of Luke's Gospel. There is no particular virtue in being old; all one has to do is not die, a thing we do not have much control over, but best accomplished by not doing stupid stuff while we're young. However, age coupled with trust in God is a thing to be sought after.

Here's a brief inventory of the trust of the elders in this story…

Zachariah - not so much, because he doubted Gabriel's prophecy of him fathering John the Baptist at his advanced age. Even so, St. Elizabeth responded to Zachariah's amorous advances and John the Baptist was born nine months later.

Elizabeth - the mother of John the Baptist, bore the shame of being childless her entire life without giving up her trust in God. And there is this remarkable bit whereupon meeting the now pregnant Mary, Elizabeth proclaims, "Why is it granted to me that the mother of *my Lord* should come to me?" (Luke 1:43, emphasis mine), becoming the first person to recognize Jesus as Lord.

Simeon - "... this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel , and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ" (Luke 2:25-26). Upon seeing the infant Jesus in the Temple, "he took him up in his arms (presumably with Mary and Joseph's permission) and blessed God and said, 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word;for my eyes have seen your salvation" (Luke 2:28-30).

Anna - she is the last on our list as she is the last to appear in the temple scene. She was a widow for most of her life, only being married for 7 years, and she was a prophetess. She spent all of her time in the Temple fasting and praying. Although we do not have her words, St. Luke tells us, "Coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of [Jesus] to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem" (Luke 2:38).

What ties these people together is not just their advanced years. Oh, sure, they were elderly, but as I said earlier, there is precious little virtue in increasing age. The important thing is what you do with the time given. Without much in the way of assurances, all of these people held firmly to their trust in what God had promised them.

One of the keys to the Christen life well-lived is continued trust in Our Father, his Son our Lord and Savior, and the work of the Holy Spirit. Trust in spite of politics, economics, and plagues. He is true to his word. His word is established forever and heaven and earth will pass away before Our Father's promises will pass away.

As to the fascinating thing I learned: Sadly, I couldn't figure out how to add it in, so I'll just tell you. According to the traditions of the Church, St. Luke, in addition to writing the "Gospel of Luke" and "The Acts of the Apostles," also produced icons (properly speaking, St. Luke *authored* or *wrote* icons). Perhaps the most famous are *Our Lady of Vladimir*  (included) and *Black Madonna of Częstochowa*. The Saint Thomas Christians of India claim to still have one of the Theotokos icons that Saint Luke painted and which Saint Thomas brought to India.

Apparently this is widely known, but not by me. I am FASCINATED! Still, as fascinating as this is, it does not compare to the delight of knowing Our Father is true to his word and can be trusted.

The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always.
paul+
